_meta.note: Source language. Strings are authored here; every other catalogue translates this one. Clinical terms follow standard English usage (deuteranomaly, protanomaly, tritanomaly).

app.name: Colorblind Me
app.intro: Every colour-blindness simulator shows the most severe case. Three people in four see far better than that. Measure the real figure, then show it.
app.privacy: Everything runs in your browser. No measurement is sent anywhere, and the vision code travels inside the link itself.

measure.title: I am colour blind
measure.desc: Three minutes of measurement, and you leave with a code that describes your vision.

view.title: I want to see what someone sees
view.desc: Enter the code you were given. The camera shows the world the way they see it.

setup.title: One condition only
setup.filters: Turn off every colour filter. Night mode, adaptive brightness, f.lux, accessibility colour correction, a "vivid" display profile. These apply after the page and would corrupt the measurement.
setup.brightness: Brightness between half and three quarters, at arm's length.
setup.ambient: Steady ambient light, no glare on the panel.
setup.botheyes: Both eyes open, as in normal use.
setup.honesty: When you see nothing, say so. It is the most useful answer in the test.
setup.gamma_hint: Step back and squint: both halves should tend towards the same lightness.

result.title: Your vision, in two numbers
result.gap: Your severity is {factor} times lower than what standard simulators show. That gap is exactly what makes people say "oh, you poor thing".
result.code_hint: The code travels inside the link: the people you send it to just open it and see. Nothing to install, no account.
result.gap_sub: less severe than what they display
result.axis_from_luminance: The axis was decided on luminance, which is the only signal that separates protan from deutan reliably. The severity comes from the chromatic staircase.

load.title: Someone's vision code
load.intro: If you were sent a link, it is already loaded and there is nothing to type. Otherwise, enter the code here.
load.label: Vision code
load.preset_warning: A preset is an average. If the person you have in mind can measure themselves, their code will always be better.
load.invalid: That code is not recognised. Check the letters and digits.

view.drag: Drag the handle. One side is what you see, the other what they see — measured, not guessed.
view.severity_hint: Moving this slider leaves the measurement behind. The marker stays on the real value.
view.standard_desc: Severity 1.0: everything merges. Nobody sees this.
view.nocode: No vision code in this link. Pick a preset below, or paste the code you were given — a preset is only an average.
view.badimage: That image could not be read. Try another file.
view.triptych: Show all three side by side
view.triptych_hint: Original, the measured vision, and what off-the-shelf simulators display. Useful for making the argument; unnecessary for simply looking.
view.typical_desc: What the person looking at this sees.
view.measured_desc: The measured vision. Colours shift, but they do not all collapse together.

camera.notfound: No camera found on this device.
camera.busy: The camera is already in use by another application.
camera.framed: This page is running inside an embedded frame, which does not grant camera permission: open it in its own tab.
camera.fallback: Load a photo instead — the result is the same, just less alive.
camera.insecure: The camera needs a secure connection. This page is being served over plain http, where browsers block camera access outright.
camera.unsupported: This browser does not offer the camera to web pages. Browsers built on Android's system WebView — LineageOS's Jelly among them — cannot grant camera access at all, and refuse without ever asking. Chrome or Firefox will work.
camera.timeout: The camera never answered — no prompt, no refusal. That is the signature of a WebView-based browser denying the request silently. Try Chrome or Firefox.
camera.unknown: The camera could not be started.

limits.title: What this measurement does not tell you
limits.notdiag: This is not a diagnosis. The protocol fits a model to your discrimination; it replaces neither a Nagel anomaloscope nor a CAD test.
limits.confusion: It conveys your confusions, not your experience. No image can show what a red looks like to you.
limits.notpoorer: What looks impoverished to the viewer is not impoverished to you: they compare it to the original, and you never had that comparison.
limits.screens: It depends on two screens. You calibrate on yours; others look on theirs.
limits.protan: For a protan it underestimates: the protocol neutralises luminance cues, which is precisely what protanopia takes away.
limits.onenumber: One number does not sum up an eye: macular pigment, lens ageing with age, the size of the coloured field, ambient light.

lum.learn_title: The question is counter-intuitive. Let's see it once.
lum.learn_lead: You will be asked which of two squares would be the paler grey in a black and white photograph. Here is what that means:
lum.learn_point: The red pulls the eye harder. The grey is the paler one. It is the grey you would pick. Not "which do I see best", not "which stands out from the background", not "which is more colourful".
lum.squint: The trick that works: squint hard until it blurs. Hue fades before lightness does, and only what you are being asked to judge is left.
lum.ask: The paler one in black and white
lum.howto: Squint. If you cannot tell them apart, say so — that is an answer, not a failure.
lum.undecided: The lightness ratio fell in the undecided band, so the axis is a guess rather than a measurement. Run the measurement again in better light before trusting it.
